subject: VAN CREVELD (1954)
object: VAN CREVELD (1954) reported on congenital idiopathic hypoprothrombinemia.

subject: QUICK et al. (1955)
object: QUICK et al. (1955) reported on congenital hypoprothrombinemic states.

subject: POOL et al. (1962)
object: POOL et al. (1962) reported severe congenital hypoprothrombinemia in a Black boy.

subject: JOSSO et al. (1962)
object: JOSSO et al. (1962) studied a case of congenital hypoprothrombinemia.

subject: QUICK and HUSSEY (1962)
object: QUICK and HUSSEY (1962) reported on hereditary hypoprothrombinemias, meaning inherited deficiencies of prothrombin.

subject: Lanchantin et al. (1968)
object: Lanchantin et al. (1968) studied the amino acid composition of human plasma prothrombin.

subject: Shapiro et al. (1969)
object: Shapiro et al. (1969) studied a large family in which 11 members had half-normal plasma levels of biologic prothrombin activity but normal quantities of immunoreactive prothrombin, whose immunologic properties appeared identical to those of the normal zymogen.

subject: Shapiro et al. (1969)
object: Shapiro et al. (1969) found the pattern of inheritance of dysprothrombinemia in the family to be autosomal, and suggested that affected individuals were heterozygotes.

subject: Shapiro et al. (1969)
object: Shapiro et al. (1969) isolated prothrombin from the plasma of an affected individual and obtained normal protein yields but half-normal prothrombin activity; activation via intrinsic and extrinsic systems, concentrated sodium citrate, or trypsin yielded half or less of the expected thrombin clotting and esterase activities. During clotting all prothrombin-mobility material disappeared, and serum immunoelectrophoresis showed a normal 'pro piece' plus an additional activation product of intermediate mobility.

subject: Shapiro et al. (1969)
object: Shapiro et al. (1969) concluded that in affected heterozygotes half of the synthesized prothrombin molecules are structurally abnormal, undergoing some alterations during activation but being incapable of releasing active thrombin.

subject: Kattlove et al. (1970)
object: Kattlove et al. (1970) reported on hereditary prothrombin deficiency.

subject: Josso et al. (1971)
object: Josso et al. (1971) described a congenital abnormality of the prothrombin (factor II) molecule, which they called prothrombin Barcelona, in 4 sibs.

subject: Girolami (1971)
object: Girolami (1971) studied the hereditary transmission of congenital 'true' hypoprothrombinemia.

subject: Girolami et al. (1974)
object: Girolami et al. (1974) described prothrombin Padua, which they called a 'new' congenital dysprothrombinemia.

subject: F2 Prothrombin Padua
object: F2

subject: Owen et al. (1978)
object: Owen et al. (1978) restudied one of the first patients identified by Quick and colleagues as having a plasma prothrombin defect. She had about half the normal amount of prothrombin antigen but almost no prothrombin function. The authors proposed calling this dysprothrombin 'prothrombin Quick.'

subject: Owen et al. (1978)
object: Owen et al. (1978) found that a second patient first described by Quick had true hypoprothrombinemia, lacking both functional and antigenic prothrombin.

subject: Owen et al. (1978)
object: Owen et al. (1978) reviewed the reported inherited prothrombin defects. There were 10 families with hypoprothrombinemia (true reductions of prothrombin), 6 families with dysprothrombinemia (functionally abnormal prothrombin), and 8 more families with a prothrombin abnormality that had not yet been classified.

subject: Rabiet et al. (1979)
object: Rabiet et al. (1979) studied the activation of the abnormal prothrombin variant prothrombin Barcelona and reported evidence that active high molecular weight intermediates form during its activation.

subject: F2 prothrombin Barcelona
object: F2

subject: Weinger et al. (1980)
object: Weinger et al. (1980) described a 72-year-old man with a lifelong history of easy bruisability and posttraumatic bleeding who had a prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time. His plasma Stypven, Taipan, and Echis carinatus venom clotting times were also prolonged. The variant was named prothrombin Houston.

subject: Weinger et al. (1980)
object: Weinger et al. (1980) confirmed a dysprothrombin in their patient by a discrepancy between plasma prothrombin coagulant activity and prothrombin antigen levels. The prothrombin was fully adsorbed to and eluted from barium sulfate, and on crossed immunoelectrophoresis it resembled normal prothrombin, but crossed immunoelectrofocusing showed the patient's prothrombin antigen was more basic than normal.

subject: Weinger et al. (1980)
object: Weinger et al. (1980) found that the patient's barium sulfate eluate, activated by Echis carinatus venom, clotted purified fibrinogen more slowly than normal eluate, although SDS gel electrophoresis showed the prothrombin was cleaved by the venom. They suggested that the coagulopathy of prothrombin Houston results from the generation of a dysfunctional thrombin.

subject: Smith et al. (1981)
object: Smith et al. (1981) described a pair of identical twins with dysprothrombinemia (prothrombin Gainesville) who were evaluated for menometrorrhagia and mild postoperative bleeding. Each twin had a slightly prolonged partial thromboplastin time and prothrombin time. Apart from this, the full hemostatic evaluation was normal.

subject: Smith et al. (1981)
object: Smith et al. (1981) found that plasma prothrombin activity in the identical twins with prothrombin Gainesville was 23% and 25% of normal by a Russell's viper venom assay. However, each twin had 70% of normal plasma prothrombin antigen, which indicated a dysprothrombinemia. The authors stated that prothrombin Gainesville was the twelfth such dysprothrombin reported.

subject: Smith et al. (1981)
object: Smith et al. (1981) obtained prothrombin kinetic data in the twins before and during hysterectomy. Infused prothrombin (Konyne) had a volume of distribution of about 1.5 times the plasma volume and a half-life of 34 hours.

subject: Board et al. (1982)
object: Board et al. (1982) described a new electrophoretic procedure for localizing prothrombin that revealed 3 allelic variants at the prothrombin structural locus (FII). In each case, investigation of the activated products showed that the structural variation was located on a profragment and not on the enzymatically active thrombin molecule.

subject: Board et al. (1982)
object: Board et al. (1982) found that one prothrombin electrophoretic variant allele, FII4, reached polymorphic frequencies in some Pacific Island populations.

subject: F2 FII4
object: F2

subject: Josso et al. (1982)
object: Josso et al. (1982) studied a French family with a mild hemorrhagic tendency. The father was heterozygous for hypoprothrombinemia and the mother was heterozygous for dysprothrombinemia. All possible genetic combinations were seen among the children, and 3 of them were double heterozygotes.

subject: Josso et al. (1982)
object: Josso et al. (1982) identified an abnormal prothrombin, which they named prothrombin Metz, in 3 children of a French family who were double heterozygotes. Each child carried hypoprothrombinemia inherited from the father and dysprothrombinemia inherited from the mother.

subject: F2 prothrombin Metz
object: F2

subject: Josso et al. (1982)
object: Josso et al. (1982) found that prothrombin Metz generated an abnormal thrombin. This thrombin was less sensitive to inactivation by antithrombin III than normal thrombin.

subject: Rubio et al. (1983)
object: Rubio et al. (1983) described a Cuban family with congenital dysprothrombinemia (prothrombin Habana). The proband, a 5-year-old girl, had umbilical bleeding after birth, then easy bruising and a bleeding tendency throughout her life. Her prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time were prolonged.

subject: Rubio et al. (1983)
object: Rubio et al. (1983) found that the proband's prothrombin activity was below 10% in several one- and two-stage assays, whereas staphylocoagulase-complexed prothrombin and immunologic methods gave levels of about 50%. The abnormal prothrombin migrated more anodically on single and two-dimensional immunoelectrophoresis, and adding calcium did not change its migration.

subject: Rubio et al. (1983)
object: In family studies, Rubio et al. (1983) found that the father had about 50% prothrombin activity and antigen (a true deficiency). The mother had 45% prothrombin activity but about 100% prothrombin antigen (a dysfunctional prothrombin). The authors suggested that the proband was heterozygous for an abnormal prothrombin and heterozygous for true prothrombin deficiency.

subject: Shirakami and Kawauchi (1984)
object: Shirakami and Kawauchi (1984) reported on congenital dysprothrombinemia.

subject: Rabiet et al. (1984)
object: Rabiet et al. (1984) purified thrombin Metz, made by activating the variant prothrombin Metz with factor Xa in the presence of calcium, phospholipid, and factor Va. By physicochemical criteria it was identical to normal thrombin. It had less than 4% of normal fibrinogen clotting activity, abnormal Km and Kcat on S2238, and only 34% of normal DAPA fluorescence enhancement. It was less than 5% as effective as normal thrombin at inducing platelet aggregation.

subject: Rabiet et al. (1984)
object: Rabiet et al. (1984) found that thrombin Metz released both fibrinopeptides A and B more slowly than normal, with fibrinopeptide B more affected, which led to slow fibrin polymerization. Its interaction with antithrombin III was slower than normal, but not in the presence of heparin. Thrombin Metz also bound less tightly to heparin-Sepharose, and heparin inhibited its activity on S2238 less strongly. The authors predicted that the defect affects the catalytic site or its vicinity and, jointly or consequently, the region that interacts with antithrombin III and heparin.

object: F2

subject: Rocha et al. (1986)
object: Rocha et al. (1986) described a 21-year-old man with congenital dysprothrombinemia who presented with hemarthrosis of the left knee together with an extensive hematoma after minor trauma. His prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time were prolonged. His parents were consanguineous.

subject: Rocha et al. (1986)
object: Rocha et al. (1986) found that the propositus had very low prothrombin activity with physiological activators (7% by one-stage and 20% by two-stage assay), Russell viper venom-cephalin (23%), Notechis scutatus scutatus venom (15%) and Echis carinatus venom (17%). By contrast, levels were borderline to normal with Taipan venom (64%) and normal by staphylocoagulase and immunologic methods, which points to a dysfunctional prothrombin molecule.

subject: Rocha et al. (1986)
object: Rocha et al. (1986) found that the propositus's consanguineous parents both had prothrombin levels reduced by 50% when physiological activators or Echis carinatus venom were used. This is consistent with both parents being heterozygous carriers.

subject: Rocha et al. (1986)
object: Rocha et al. (1986) observed a line of identity between normal and abnormal prothrombin on immunodiffusion. The abnormal prothrombin migrated less anodically, and adding calcium did not change its migration. On bidimensional immunoelectrophoresis the patient's serum showed 3 bands, compared with 2 in normal serum. The authors proposed the name prothrombin Segovia for this variant.

subject: Dumont et al. (1987)
object: Dumont et al. (1987) described a newborn girl with congenital dysprothrombinemia (prothrombin Poissy) who had severe bleeding from the second day of life. Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time were very prolonged.

subject: Dumont et al. (1987)
object: In the proband, Dumont et al. (1987) found prothrombin activity of about 2% in a one-stage assay. Activity was 35% with staphylocoagulase and 25% with Echis carinatus venom. Prothrombin antigen was 47%, and the protein migrated abnormally on crossed immunoelectrophoresis. In a thrombin generation system free of natural inhibitors, the abnormal prothrombin was activated slowly and incompletely. The authors called it a 'lazy' dysprothrombin.

subject: Dumont et al. (1987)
object: In a family study, Dumont et al. (1987) found both normal and abnormal prothrombin in the plasma of the proband's father, mother, and brother. They suggested that the proband was homozygous for the dysprothrombin.

subject: Inomoto et al. (1987)
object: Inomoto et al. (1987) purified a mutant prothrombin, designated prothrombin Tokushima, from the plasma of a proband with 12% of normal plasma prothrombin clotting activity and 42% of normal prothrombin antigen. The purified variant had the same SDS-PAGE mobility as normal prothrombin, and its proteolysis catalyzed by factor Xa was identical to that of normal prothrombin.

subject: F2 prothrombin Tokushima
object: F2

subject: Inomoto et al. (1987)
object: Inomoto et al. (1987) found that thrombin Tokushima, generated by factor Xa activation, had normal molecular weight but less than 22% of normal clotting activity and a kcat/Km toward a fluorogenic substrate less than one-tenth of normal, although active-site titration showed no difference from normal thrombin. Thrombin Tokushima was 2.5% as effective as normal thrombin in inducing platelet aggregation and 33% as effective in forming a complex with antithrombin III. The authors concluded that the molecular defect resides in the thrombin portion of the prothrombin and that binding sites for various substrates appear greatly impaired.

subject: Valls-de-Ruiz et al. (1987)
object: Valls-de-Ruiz et al. (1987) found a functionally normal but structurally abnormal prothrombin variant in a Mexican family and named it prothrombin 'Mexico City.' On immunoisoelectric focusing, the variant had a more acidic isoelectric point (4.01) than normal prothrombin (4.29). Its molecular weight on SDS-PAGE was normal. Two-dimensional immunoelectrophoresis showed abnormal cleavage by factor Xa and by Echis carinatus venom, although both produced functionally normal thrombin. Calcium binding and overall antigenic structure were normal.

subject: F2 Prothrombin Mexico City
object: F2

subject: Valls-de-Ruiz et al. (1987)
object: Valls-de-Ruiz et al. (1987) suggested that prothrombin Mexico City results from a simple substitution or translocation mutation at the level of fragment 2. They considered the variant different from previously described prothrombin variants.

subject: Valls-de-Ruiz et al. (1987)
object: Valls-de-Ruiz et al. (1987) described prothrombin Mexico City as an asymptomatic prothrombin variant with autosomal dominant inheritance.

subject: Lutze et al. (1989)
object: Lutze et al. (1989) described dysprothrombinemia (prothrombin Magdeburg) in 7 members of 1 family spanning 3 generations. Five of the 7 had a slightly increased bleeding tendency, seen mainly as heavier or prolonged bleeding after trauma and surgery.

subject: Lutze et al. (1989)
object: Lutze et al. (1989) found that in the affected family members, the ratio of factor II clotting activity to factor II concentration was reduced to about 0.5. This reduction was not seen when prothrombin was measured after activation with staphylocoagulase. SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis showed 'normal' prothrombin plus 2 abnormal prothrombins with higher molecular weights and lower isoelectric points.

subject: Lutze et al. (1989)
object: Lutze et al. (1989) concluded that prothrombin Magdeburg is an autosomal hereditary dysprothrombinemia and that the affected persons are heterozygotes.

subject: Iwahana et al. (1992)
object: Iwahana et al. (1992) analyzed the prothrombin gene in a proband who was a compound heterozygote for dysprothrombinemia (prothrombin Tokushima) and hypoprothrombinemia. Using PCR-SSCP with endonuclease digestion and mutated primer-mediated PCR-RFLP, they detected a single nucleotide substitution responsible for prothrombin Tokushima, along with three polymorphisms.

subject: F2 prothrombin Tokushima single nucleotide substitution

subject: Iwahana et al. (1992)
object: Iwahana et al. (1992) identified the hypoprothrombinemia allele in the compound heterozygous proband as a single base insertion of thymine at position 4177 in exon 6 of the prothrombin gene, found by PCR-SSCP with endonuclease digestion and genomic sequencing. The frameshift altered the amino acid sequence from codon 114 and created a premature TGA stop at codon 174 in exon 7; because exon 7 encodes the kringle 2 domain preceding the thrombin sequence, the authors concluded this leads to a null prothrombin phenotype. Inheritance of this allele from the father was demonstrated.

object: F2

subject: Iwahana et al. (1992)
object: Iwahana et al. (1992) used PCR-SSCP, PCR-RFLP and sequencing of PCR-amplified genomic DNA to study the dysprothrombinemia variant prothrombin Tokushima. They found a C-to-T substitution at nucleotide 9,490 that changed arginine to tryptophan at position 418 (Arg418Trp) and abolished an MspI site. The proband had inherited the mutant gene from the mother. The authors considered this point mutation the likely molecular basis because Southern blot analysis showed no distinct changes, the variant gene product had the same molecular weight as the abnormal protein, and the proteolytic peptide fragments showed no other amino acid abnormalities.

subject: F2 c.9490C>T / p.R418W
object: F2

subject: Iwahana et al. (1992)
object: Iwahana et al. (1992) concluded that PCR-SSCP and PCR-RFLP (loss of an MspI site) were useful for detecting the abnormal prothrombin gene and for direct diagnosis of carrier status in dysprothrombinemia. The authors stated that this was the first report of gene analysis of dysprothrombinemia.

subject: Morishita et al. (1992)
object: Morishita et al. (1992) described Prothrombin Himi, an inherited dysfunctional prothrombin. It had reduced fibrinogen clotting activity but kept full hydrolytic activity toward synthetic substrates.

subject: Morishita et al. (1992)
object: In a female proband with Prothrombin Himi, Morishita et al. (1992) amplified exons 8 to 14 of the prothrombin gene by PCR and screened them by SSCP analysis. Sequencing then found compound heterozygosity for two new point mutations in exon 10. The first was a T-to-C transition at nucleotide 8751 that changed methionine to threonine at codon 337 (Met337Thr; Thrombin Himi I), inherited from the father. The second was a G-to-A transition at nucleotide 8904 that changed arginine to histidine at codon 388 (Arg388His; Thrombin Himi II), inherited from the mother. One of the proband's sisters also inherited both variant alleles.

subject: Morishita et al. (1992)
object: Morishita et al. (1992) found that the Prothrombin Himi proband's second prothrombin allele carried a G-to-A transition at nucleotide 8904 in exon 10. This change replaced arginine with histidine at codon 388 (Arg388His; Thrombin Himi II) and was inherited from her mother. Together with Met337Thr from her father, it made the proband compound heterozygous for two dysfunctional prothrombin molecules.

subject: F2 c.8904G>A / p.R388H

subject: Poort et al. (1994)
object: Poort et al. (1994) described a male patient with a severe bleeding tendency and hypoprothrombinemia (factor II activity 2%, factor II antigen 5%). Five homozygous brothers and sisters of the propositus were also clinically affected, with severe hemorrhages including epistaxis and soft tissue, muscle, and joint bleeding in all, and severe hemorrhages in the 2 women.

subject: Poort et al. (1994)
object: In a patient with severe hypoprothrombinemia, Poort et al. (1994) identified by direct sequencing of the prothrombin gene a homozygous A-to-G substitution in exon 3, predicting a tyr44-to-cys (Y44C; TAC-to-TGC) substitution. Both parents were heterozygous, and family studies showed complete cosegregation of the mutation with prothrombin deficiency; only the homozygous sibs were clinically affected.

subject: Poort et al. (1994)
object: Poort et al. (1994) concluded that the bleeding tendency in this family appeared to be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, since only homozygous family members were clinically affected and the parents were heterozygous.

subject: Girolami et al. (1998)
object: Girolami et al. (1998) noted that Quick et al. first described prothrombin (factor II) deficiency in 1947, and that Shapiro et al. reported the first prothrombin abnormality in 1969. The condition is still considered very rare.

subject: Girolami et al. (1998)
object: Girolami et al. (1998) stated that prothrombin deficiency or abnormality can be diagnosed with a combination of clotting, chromogenic and immunologic assays. In true deficiency, all assays decrease in parallel whatever the activating agent. Discrepancies among clotting assays, particularly with viper venoms, suggest dysprothrombinemia. The authors stated that cases with a parallel decrease in prothrombin activity and antigen should not be considered examples of hypoprothrombinemia.

subject: Girolami et al. (1998)
object: Girolami et al. (1998) reported that factor II activity is usually less than 10% of normal in homozygotes for true deficiency and 40 to 60% in heterozygotes. In congenital dysprothrombinemia, factor II levels are more variable, usually 1 to 50% of normal, because patients may be homozygotes, heterozygotes, or compound heterozygotes. Compound heterozygotes may carry an abnormality plus a true deficiency, or two distinct abnormalities. Antigen levels in dysprothrombinemia are normal, near normal or slightly decreased, but always higher than clotting activity.

subject: Girolami et al. (1998)
object: Girolami et al. (1998) reported that bleeding can be severe in homozygous true prothrombin deficiency, with hemarthroses and intracranial bleeding described. Bleeding is more variable in dysprothrombinemias, and heterozygotes are usually asymptomatic. Prognosis is variable and generally matches the prothrombin activity level.

subject: Girolami et al. (1998)
object: Girolami et al. (1998) stated that substitution therapy uses prothrombin complex concentrates or plasma. Because infused prothrombin has a long half-life of about 70 hours, hemostatically effective levels of about 50% of normal are easily achieved.

subject: Girolami et al. (1998)
object: Girolami et al. (1998) noted that the prothrombin gene is located on chromosome 11 and is composed of 10 exons. They reported that molecular studies have found several point mutations in some dysprothrombinemias.

subject: Lefkowitz et al. (2000)
object: Lefkowitz et al. (2000) described the original patient with prothrombin Denver. The patient had a severe hemophilia-like bleeding disorder and was treated with weekly prophylactic factor replacement. Factor II activity was 5 units/dl and factor II antigen was 21 units/dl, consistent with moderately severe dysprothrombinemia.

subject: Lefkowitz et al. (2000)
object: In the prothrombin Denver patient, Lefkowitz et al. (2000) sequenced PCR-amplified prothrombin exons (the entire thrombin portion, exons VIII-XIV, and exons I-II and IV-VII) and found compound heterozygosity for two different Glu-to-Lys point mutations, glu300-to-lys and glu309-to-lys. DNA was also obtained from the patient's mother and brother.

subject: Lefkowitz et al. (2000)
object: Lefkowitz et al. (2000) assayed plasma from the prothrombin Denver proband, and the results suggested that the functional defect was in the activation of the zymogen to the enzyme.

subject: Lefkowitz et al. (2000)
object: Lefkowitz et al. (2000) noted that dysprothrombinemia is a rare congenital cause of bleeding, and that fewer than 25 families with a functional prothrombin (factor II) defect had been reported.

subject: Akhavan et al. (2000)
object: Akhavan et al. (2000) described prothrombin deficiency as an autosomal recessive disorder with a moderately severe bleeding tendency.

subject: Akhavan et al. (2000)
object: Akhavan et al. (2000) screened the prothrombin gene in 13 patients with prothrombin deficiency and found 9 novel candidate mutations. Of the 11 patients with hypoprothrombinemia, 10 were homozygous for 5 mutations and 1 was a compound heterozygote. The 2 patients with dysprothrombinemia were homozygous for 2 mutations. Eight mutations were missense: Arg-1Gln and Arg-2Trp in the propeptide, Asp118Try in kringle-1, Arg220Cys in kringle-2, and Gly330Ser, Ser354Arg, Arg382His and Arg538Cys in the serine protease domain. The ninth was an in-frame 3-bp deletion that removed one amino acid (del Lys301/302).

subject: Akhavan et al. (2000)
object: Akhavan et al. (2000) mapped the missense mutations onto crystal structures of alpha-thrombin and prothrombin fragments 1 and 2. They inferred that the hypoprothrombinemia mutations affected cleavage of the propeptide from the Gla domain, the stability of kringle-1 and kringle-2, or the close association of the A and B chains of the serine protease domain. They inferred that the dysprothrombinemia mutations directly impaired catalytic function because they lie at the active site crevice or exosite 1 of the serine protease domain.

subject: Meeks and Abshire (2008)
object: Meeks and Abshire (2008) reviewed prothrombin (factor II) deficiency, a rare autosomal recessive coagulation disorder. Prothrombin is activated to thrombin, which cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin and contributes to a stable fibrin clot. They noted that more than 40 prothrombin mutations were known and that both hypoprothrombinemia and dysprothrombinemia had been described.

subject: Meeks and Abshire (2008)
object: Meeks and Abshire (2008) stated that prothrombin deficiency occurs in about 1 in 1 to 2 million people.

subject: Meeks and Abshire (2008)
object: Meeks and Abshire (2008) noted that bleeding in prothrombin deficiency is mostly mucosal or follows surgery or trauma, but joint bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage had also been reported.

subject: Meeks and Abshire (2008)
object: Meeks and Abshire (2008) noted that low prothrombin activity usually prolongs both the activated partial thromboplastin time and the prothrombin time. The hemostatic level of prothrombin is thought to be 20 to 40%, and its half-life is about 3 days.

subject: Meeks and Abshire (2008)
object: Meeks and Abshire (2008) stated that no purified prothrombin products were available for replacement therapy. Fresh frozen plasma and prothrombin complex concentrates both contain prothrombin and may be used for treatment.

subject: Segal et al. (2009)
object: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 46 articles, Segal et al. (2009) found that, in probands with venous thromboembolism, heterozygosity for prothrombin G20210A did not predict recurrent VTE compared with individuals without the variant (OR 1.45; 95% CI 0.96-2.2). They concluded that the evidence was insufficient on whether G20210A homozygosity predicts recurrent VTE and on the risk of VTE in family members of carriers.

subject: Lancellotti and De Cristofaro (2009)
object: Lancellotti and De Cristofaro (2009) reviewed congenital prothrombin deficiency and described 2 main phenotypes. Hypoprothrombinemia (type I deficiency) has low levels of both prothrombin activity and antigen. Dysprothrombinemia (type II deficiency) has normal or near-normal synthesis of a dysfunctional protein. Hypoprothrombinemia together with dysprothrombinemia had also been described in compound heterozygotes.

subject: Lancellotti and De Cristofaro (2009)
object: Lancellotti and De Cristofaro (2009) stated that prothrombin deficiency is among the rarest inherited coagulation disorders, with a prevalence of about 1 in 2,000,000. No living patient with undetectable plasma prothrombin had been reported.

subject: Lancellotti and De Cristofaro (2009)
object: Lancellotti and De Cristofaro (2009) reported that 40 different mutations had been identified in prothrombin deficiency. Many clustered around the catalytic site, and another hot spot was in anion binding exosite I (the fibrinogen recognition site). More recently, mutations had also been found in the Na(+)-binding loop and in the thrombin light A chain. Most hypoprothrombinemia-associated mutations were missense, but nonsense mutations and 1 single-nucleotide deletion had also been described.
